analysis.one_liner: Froze most major federal regulations until unemployment fell to 6% and added cost hurdles to financial and environmental rules.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 245-172 on July 26, 2012, but the Senate never voted, and it died when that Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have banned federal agencies from issuing any significant new rule — a rule costing the economy $50 million or more, or materially affecting health, safety, the environment, or jobs — until unemployment averaged 6% or less for a quarter, something it had not done since 2008. It would also have barred costly rules issued between a presidential election and a new president's inauguration, made it harder for groups to settle lawsuits that force agencies to act, set strict deadlines for environmental reviews with permits automatically approved if agencies miss them, and required the SEC and commodities regulator to clear new rules through cost-benefit analysis while voiding the SEC's climate-disclosure guidance. Supporters framed it as job relief for small business; the practical effect was to pause most new public-protection rules during a period of high unemployment.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries — banks and securities firms facing new financial rules, energy and infrastructure developers facing environmental reviews, and manufacturers facing major rules — would gain years of delay or outright blocking of new requirements. Small businesses that sue over federal rules would get their attorney's fees paid out of agency budgets.

how_it_helps.text: Title I bars any 'significant regulatory action' — anything costing the economy $50 million a year or materially affecting the economy, jobs, environment, or public health — until the Labor Secretary reports a quarter averaging 6.0% unemployment or less, with exemptions only for emergencies, criminal and civil-rights enforcement, national security, trade agreements, and rule repeals [S5][S6].

Title II blocks agencies from proposing or finalizing major 'midnight rules' during the window between a presidential election and a new president's inauguration, targeting outgoing administrations' final rules [S5][S6].

Titles VI and VII require the SEC and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to adopt rules only after a 'reasoned determination' that benefits justify costs, with alternatives analysis and post-implementation review, and Section 604 declares the SEC's existing climate-disclosure guidance null and void and bars future guidance on the subject [S5][S6].

Title V requires environmental impact statements to be completed within two years, limits agencies to one statement and one assessment per project, lets project sponsors prepare environmental documents, and deems a permit approved if an agency misses its deadline; it also bars most lawsuits unless the challenger commented during review and files within 180 days [S5][S6].

Title III adds public-comment, intervention, and Attorney General approval requirements to consent decrees and settlements that force agencies to issue rules, making it harder for outside groups to negotiate deadlines for agency action [S5][S6].

Section 104(d) requires courts to award attorney's fees to substantially prevailing small businesses (500 or fewer employees or under $7 million net worth) that sue under the freeze, paid out of the budget of the office that took the challenged action [S6].

analysis.who_pays: The people regulations protect — workers facing unsafe conditions, consumers and investors facing financial misconduct, and communities facing pollution — would wait out the freeze without new protections. Agency budgets would also absorb attorney-fee awards.

drawbacks.text: The freeze would have applied to almost every rule affecting health, safety, the environment, or jobs, and with unemployment above 6% throughout 2012 it could have lasted years; the $50 million cost trigger is small relative to the entire economy, so even broadly beneficial rules would be caught [S5][S6].

Deeming permits approved when agencies miss deadlines, and limiting court challenges to prior commenters within 180 days, would remove checks on projects with environmental impacts rather than fixing delays [S5][S6].

Supporters' strongest point is real: major rules impose compliance costs that fall on hiring, small firms bear disproportionate paperwork burdens, and environmental reviews can take years; the bill's authors argued agencies should prove benefits justify costs before acting [S5][S6]. But the bill's answer — a blanket freeze keyed to one unemployment number — applies the same brake to trivial risks as to serious ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Some provisions — faster permitting coordination, retrospective review of old rules, plain-language rules — address genuine frustrations. But the centerpiece, a freeze on all significant rulemaking until unemployment hit 6%, would have suspended new public-health, safety, environmental, and financial protections indefinitely during exactly the period when people are most exposed, while the automatic permit approvals and litigation limits in the environmental title shift risk from project sponsors to the public. The costs to ordinary people outweigh the targeted efficiencies.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 245-172 in July 2012, but the Senate never brought it up for a vote — it just sat on the Senate calendar until that Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Introduced February 17, 2012, the bill was referred to both the Oversight and Government Reform and Judiciary Committees; Judiciary ordered it reported 15-13 and later 21-16, and Oversight reported it as Part II of H. Rept. 112-461 [S1][S8].

The House debated it July 25-26, 2012 under a rule that allowed only specified amendments; Democratic amendments from Hastings, Kucinich, Welch, Markey, Watt, Maloney, Woolsey, George Miller, and others were defeated, and only a handful of amendments prevailed [S8].

A Democratic motion to recommit — seeking to exempt rules on foreign-account disclosure, middle-class tax cuts, prescription drug safety, and foreclosure relief — failed 181-234, with 233 of 240 Republicans voting no and 180 of 191 Democrats voting yes [S9].
Final passage came 245-172: 232 of 240 Republicans voted yes, 13 of 191 Democrats yes, and 170 Democrats no [S10].

The Senate received the bill July 30, 2012, read it twice, and placed it on the calendar under General Orders; no committee referral, floor action, or vote ever followed before the 112th Congress ended January 3, 2013 [S1][S8].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies kept their authority to issue health, safety, environmental, and financial rules without the freeze, and the industries that stood to gain years of delay — financial firms, energy and infrastructure developers, and other major regulated businesses — did not get it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and the public the rules protect

for.name: Rep. Tim Griffin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and managed it on the House floor; moved for the Committee of the Whole to rise during debate.

for.name: House Republican leadership
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor under a structured rule (H. Res. 738, then H. Res. 741) that limited amendments and allowed only one motion to recommit.

for.name: Regulated-industry groups
for.what_they_did: Backed the bill's regulatory-freeze and cost-benefit framework as relief from pending rules; outside lobbying support that does not appear in the chamber record.

against.name: 170 of 191 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, offered amendments that were rejected, and moved to recommit with instructions to exempt key consumer and safety rules.

against.name: Senate leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor after it was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar; it received no vote before the Congress ended.

against.name: President Obama's administration
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as part of the House's anti-regulatory agenda during the 2012 session.

sides.party_line_note: Passage split sharply by party: 232 of 240 Republicans voted yes versus 13 of 191 Democrats; on the motion to recommit the split was nearly perfect, 180 of 191 Democrats yes and 233 of 240 Republicans no.

industries.note: The bill would have forced the SEC and CFTC through costly cost-benefit gatekeeping before any new rule and voided the SEC's climate-disclosure guidance, delaying financial and market rules put in place to protect investors. Slower or weaker rules shift risk onto investors and consumers.

Two-year deadlines for environmental reviews, sponsor-prepared environmental documents, automatic permit approval when agencies miss deadlines, and tight limits on court challenges would speed project approvals while reducing environmental scrutiny of them.

A freeze on any significant rule until 6% unemployment would have postponed rules costing $50 million or more across sectors — including health, safety, and environmental protections — for as long as joblessness stayed high.

industries.industry: Small businesses that challenge federal rules
industries.note: Mandatory attorney's fees for small businesses that substantially prevail in suits under the freeze, paid from agency budgets, would lower the cost of challenging new rules.
